documents: Kravchinsky & van der Baan (2022), Magnitude-Frequency Distributions and Slip-History Predictions for Earthquakes Using Cellular Automata and Absorbing Markov Chains, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2021JB022480 (published PDF, 18 pp.)

entry.evidence: Nonetheless, they are somewhat unsatisfactory since it has proven difficult to predict their behavior without extensive modeling or advanced statistical analyses

sequences.source_document: Kravchinsky & van der Baan 2022, JGR Solid Earth, published PDF

steps.action: Pose the question of whether long-range CA temporal statistics can be obtained without extensive CA modeling.
steps.quote: it has proven difficult to predict their behavior without extensive modeling or advanced statistical analyses

steps.action: Propose that, given a uniform stationary stress distribution and single-cell initiation, the CA's temporal dynamics are a memoryless mean-field process that an absorbing Markov chain can reproduce.
steps.quote: the proposed stochastic model is a mean-field approximation that replicates the CA temporal statistical behavior

steps.action: Derive binomial failure probabilities and build the absorbing Markov transition matrix from the CA parameters (Eqs 1-8, Figure 2), then write exhaustive-search and MCMC algorithms (Figure 3, Appendix A) and a conversion to physical time (Eq 11).
steps.quote: We can construct an (N + 1) × (N + 1) square transition matrix M from the binomial distributions P(n|m, N)

steps.action: Set the test conditions: L=256, R=16 (N=1,088), seven dissipation values, 10^6 plate updates, CA residual-stress noise, and a 4×10^6 burn-in following Serino et al. (2011).
steps.quote: We demonstrate the temporal mean-field congruence of the CA and the absorbing Markov chains

steps.action: Compute transition matrices for α = 0.05, 0.40 and 0.80 (Figure 5) and derive the expectation that large events favour slow growth and decay along the diagonal.
steps.quote: Thus, larger events are more likely if they involve relatively slow growth and decay rates, instead of rapidly fluctuating slip histories.

steps.action: Run the CA and the MCMC and record event time series in plate-update and physical time (Figure 6).
steps.quote: As the dissipation parameter increases, the average size of an event decreases.

steps.action: Compare frequency-size distributions from the exhaustive search (up to Scum=18), the MCMC and the CA, and against the mean-field s^-3/2 scaling, across dissipation values (Figure 7).
steps.quote: The exhaustive-search frequency-size distributions (black diamonds) match the MCMC (open circles) and CA (crosses) frequency-size distributions very accurately.

steps.action: Test whether the large-s spread is a finite-size or finite-sampling artifact by running L=512 and 10^7 plate updates (CA and MCMC) and 5×10^7 plate updates (MCMC only) (Appendix B, Figures B1-B2).
steps.quote: We find this spread present in the frequency-size distributions for systems of size L = 256 and L = 512

steps.action: Refine the interpretation: the spread is attributed to the discrete walk probabilities rather than to finite size, in agreement with Klein et al. (2000).
steps.quote: We propose that some amount of spread is inherent in the discrete ways an avalanche (CA) or Markov chain (MCMC) may develop

steps.action: Compare mean interevent physical times by event size between the CA and the MCMC (Figure 8).
steps.quote: The interevent times resulting from both the CA (dotted lines) and MCMC (solid curves) models are in good agreement with each other.

steps.action: Set the interevent results against the interoccurrence times of Christensen and Olami (1992) for OFC models, noting similarity but offering a stochastic interpretation.
steps.quote: find that the average interoccurrence time of large events within a cluster is very small

steps.action: Take the mean-field-theory prediction of a self-similar average slip-history scaling function (Eq 12) from crackling-noise work.
steps.quote: Systems that are close to a critical point are characterized by self-similar scaling functions

steps.action: Average slip histories by event size for the CA and the MCMC (Figure 9); find them similar and asymmetric, as the transition-matrix shape predicted.
steps.quote: Figure 9 confirms the earlier statement derived from the shape of the transition matrix M

steps.action: Scale the average slip histories by s^1/2, fit Eq 12 to obtain the nonuniversal constants A and B for the MCMC and the CA, and interpret the collapse as a critical state (Figure 10).
steps.quote: We fit Equation 12 for event sizes with the largest total number of avalanches binned

steps.action: Examine individual slip histories of the largest events in the CA and the MCMC and note their high variability (Figure 11).
steps.quote: The individual slip histories are highly variable with greater fluctuations in size.

steps.action: Overlay average slip histories on zoomed transition matrices to show a preferred walk through probability space (Figure 12); note that the MCMC is orders of magnitude faster.
steps.quote: illustrates why on average an avalanche sequences develops along a preferred walk

steps.action: Support the uniform stationary-stress premise with Naylor and Main (2008) and with stress snapshots taken from the authors' own CA runs.
steps.quote: Stationarity of the stress distribution was verified by taking model snapshots

steps.action: Extrapolate, without a test, that slip-history asymmetry in natural systems comes from the size of the initiating failure rather than from undersampling.
steps.quote: This suggests that in natural systems, the asymmetry observed in the average slip histories originates from the size of the initiation of the rupture

steps.action: Keep the claim that the absorbing-Markov MCMC replicates the long-range RJB CA's temporal statistics.
steps.quote: The MCMC models are in good agreement with the homogeneous RJB CA in terms of predicted time series, magnitude-frequency distributions, and average slip histories.

tree.answer: Temporal statistics of a long-range RJB cellular automaton: event sizes, interevent times, slip histories
Yes; CA output is counted directly
Replicate CA temporal statistics with an absorbing Markov chain
No rival models; the CA serves as reference and mean-field scaling as benchmark
The Markov model predicts frequency-size distributions, interevent times and asymmetric slip histories from the transition matrix
Conditions set in computation (α, L, R, run length)
Agreement holds across dissipation values, lattice sizes and run lengths
Kept: the MCMC is stochastically equivalent to the CA
Not assessable; no review file supplied

end.claim: The temporal avalanche dynamics of the long-range RJB CA can be replicated by an absorbing Markov chain whose transition matrix assumes a uniform stress distribution; the MCMC matches the CA in time series, magnitude-frequency distributions, interevent times and average slip histories.

decisive_move.sentence: Building the absorbing Markov transition matrix from binomial failure probabilities fixed by the CA parameters is what makes every later comparison and claim possible.

gates.evidence: The Markov-equivalence hypothesis (p. 2) directed which simulations were run. The MCMC-versus-CA comparison across seven dissipation values (pp. 8-12) could have failed, but agreement is judged visually, with no stated fit criterion. Nothing was fixed in advance; the burn-in copies Serino et al. (2011).

imports.item: Absorbing Markov chains and transition matrices (Kemeny & Snell 1960)
Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling and coin-flip binomial generator (Devroye 1986)
Integer partitions (Andrews 1976) and MATLAB permutation-with-sum code (Luong 2020) for the exhaustive search
Crackling noise / mean-field self-similar avalanche scaling function, from Barkhausen noise studies
Markov treatment of the Oslo sandpile model (Corral 2004)

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded. The paper makes no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' statement; novelty is only implied, for example by the contrast with Corral (2004) on p. 13. CA-MCMC agreement is judged visually from overlaid plots; no goodness-of-fit statistic or threshold is reported. The CA code came from Kazemian (acknowledgments); the authors did not build it. The stationarity snapshots of the CA stress are mentioned but not shown (p. 13). Sub-claims sit at other statuses: the critical-state reading from the s^1/2 collapse (p. 11) is best_explanation. The asymmetry attributed to transition-matrix asymmetry (p. 11) is best_explanation. The spread as inherent rather than a finite-sampling effect (p. 9, Appendix B) is best_explanation, partly supported by robustness runs; the 5×10^7 run is MCMC only. The natural-system statement on initiation size (p. 14) is an untested hypothesis. Inference: there is a text-caption inconsistency, with p. 11 giving α = 0.20 for Figure 9b and the caption giving 0.40. No composition fits: the walk is a model-to-model method validation, with a hypothesised approximation tested against the full simulation it simplifies.

disagreements.target: Christensen and Olami (1992): interoccurrence time as a measure of correlation buildup
disagreements.support: The Markov model reproduces the CA interevent times as a memoryless stochastic process, implying no correlation buildup is needed.
disagreements.quote: whereas our Markovian model suggests that the sequence of events originates as a stochastic process

disagreements.target: Markov-chain approaches to minimalist models (Corral 2004; Białecki 2015; Tejedor et al. 2008; Vázquez-Prada et al. 2002)
disagreements.support: Using a stationary uniform distribution instead of full configurations lets the method handle a large-N long-range CA and give avalanche sequences.
disagreements.quote: but this approach is restricted to small model sizes due to the number of configurations rapidly growing [...]

disagreements.target: Reading of the characteristic distribution (Youngs & Coppersmith 1985; Parsons et al. 2018) as implying finite-size effects in the largest [...]
disagreements.support: Appendix B runs at L=256 and L=512 show the largest events are limited by dissipation, not system size.
disagreements.quote: we demonstrate that the largest events in both CA and MCMC models are limited in growth by dissipation rather than finite size effects

disagreements.target: Position that slip-history asymmetry is an undersampling statistical artifact (cited with Ben-Zion 2008; Mehta et al. 2006)
disagreements.support: A conceptual argument from transition-matrix rows with more initiating failures; no simulation test.
disagreements.quote: rather than being an undersampling statistical artifact

alternatives_considered.chosen: Long-range RJB CA with 2D redistribution and residual-stress randomness
alternatives_considered.reason: RJB stress distribution is more uniform, supporting the uniform-stress assumption
Approximates an infinite system without border effects

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exhaustive search for small Scum and MCMC sampling for the full range
alternatives_considered.reason: The number of walks grows exponentially, so exhaustive search is limited to low Scum

alternatives_considered.chosen: Coin-flip (sum of Bernoulli trials) binomial generator
CA residual-stress noise σR = 0.0 ± 0.1 (CA only, not MCMC)
alternatives_considered.reason: Noise prevents periodic behaviour in the CA

alternatives_considered.chosen: Interevent time between events of identical size
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Interoccurrence time between subsequent events (Christensen & Olami 1992)
